title: Anti-Patterns & Code Smells
summary: Recognize the recurring red flags in object-oriented code — from God Objects to Spaghetti Code — and the refactors that fix them.

blocks.markdown:
A **code smell** is a surface symptom in code that hints at a deeper design problem — not a bug, just a warning sign.

- An **anti-pattern** is a common *solution* to a recurring problem that looks reasonable but backfires at scale.
- Smells live in a method or class; anti-patterns live in the overall structure or process.
- Both point the same way: toward refactoring, not necessarily toward "broken" code.
- Related: [solid-principles](solid-principles), [coupling-cohesion](coupling-cohesion).

blocks.subTitle: Smell vs anti-pattern
blocks.markdown:
Quick contrast before the detail.

| | Code smell | Anti-pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Method / class | Architecture / process |
| Example | Long Method | Big Ball of Mud |
| Fix | Local refactor | Structural rework |

Smells often accumulate into anti-patterns if ignored.

blocks.subTitle: Defining a code smell
blocks.markdown:
A **code smell** doesn't mean the code is wrong — it runs and passes tests. It means the code is **harder to change than it should be**.

- Coined by Kent Beck, popularized by Martin Fowler's *Refactoring*.
- Smells are **heuristics**, not proofs — they tell you where to *look*, not what to *conclude*.
- The fix for a smell is almost always a targeted **refactoring**.

blocks.subTitle: Defining an anti-pattern
blocks.markdown:
An **anti-pattern** is a solution that seemed sensible when first applied but produces more harm than the problem it solved.

- It differs from just "bad code" — it's a **named, recurring** mistake with a recognizable shape.
- Anti-patterns often start from a good instinct (reuse, flexibility, safety) taken too far.
- Each has a known **refactored path**, same as design patterns document known good ones.

blocks.subTitle: God Object / God Class
blocks.markdown:
A **God Object** is a class that knows or does too much — it accumulates fields and methods for every feature that touches it.

- Symptoms: huge class, many unrelated methods, other classes depend heavily on it.
- Violates **Single Responsibility** ([solid-principles](solid-principles)) and tanks cohesion ([coupling-cohesion](coupling-cohesion)).
- Fix: split by responsibility — Extract Class, delegate to focused collaborators.

blocks.subTitle: Long Method & Long Parameter List
blocks.markdown:
A **Long Method** tries to do several things in one block, forcing readers to hold too much context at once.

- Fix: **Extract Method** — pull cohesive chunks into named helpers.
- **Long Parameter List** — a method needs so many inputs that calls become error-prone.
- Fix: group related parameters into a small object (**Introduce Parameter Object**).

blocks.subTitle: Feature Envy
blocks.markdown:
**Feature Envy** is when a method is more interested in another class's data than its own — it calls that class's getters repeatedly to do its work.

- Sign: a method in `A` mostly reads and combines fields from `B`.
- Fix: **Move Method** — relocate the logic into the class that owns the data.

blocks.subTitle: Duplicated Code & Shotgun Surgery
blocks.markdown:
**Duplicated Code** — the same logic copy-pasted in multiple spots; a fix in one place is easy to miss in another.

- Fix: **Extract Method/Class**, or push shared behavior up via inheritance or composition.
- **Shotgun Surgery** — one small change forces edits across many files because responsibility is scattered.
- Fix: consolidate the scattered logic into a single owner class.

blocks.subTitle: Primitive Obsession & Magic Numbers
blocks.markdown:
**Primitive Obsession** — using raw strings/ints for concepts that deserve their own type (an `email` as a bare `String`, money as a `float`).

- Fix: wrap it in a small value type (`Email`, `Money`) that validates and carries behavior.
- **Magic Numbers** — unexplained literals (`if (status == 3)`) scattered through code.
- Fix: name them as constants or enum values so intent is visible.

blocks.subTitle: Data Clumps
blocks.markdown:
A **Data Clump** is a group of variables that always travel together as parameters — `street, city, zip` passed around as three separate arguments everywhere.

- If you'd delete one, you'd probably have to delete them all — that's the tell.
- Fix: bundle them into one class or struct (`Address`) and pass that instead.

blocks.subTitle: Spaghetti Code & Golden Hammer
blocks.markdown:
**Spaghetti Code** — control flow so tangled (deep nesting, gotos, scattered state) that tracing one path means tracing them all.

- Fix: introduce structure — extract methods, apply state/strategy patterns, flatten conditionals.
- **Golden Hammer** — reaching for one familiar tool or pattern for every problem, whether it fits or not.
- Fix: evaluate each problem on its own; a favorite hammer isn't always the right one.

blocks.subTitle: Lava Flow & Big Ball of Mud
blocks.markdown:
**Lava Flow** — dead code and abandoned experiments left in place because nobody's sure if they're still needed; it hardens into the codebase like cooled lava.

- Fix: verify with tests/usage data, then delete confidently.
- **Big Ball of Mud** — a system with no discernible architecture; everything can reach everything.
- Fix: incrementally carve out modules with clear boundaries — you rarely rewrite it in one shot.

blocks.subTitle: Singleton-as-global-state
blocks.markdown:
The **Singleton pattern** is legitimate for one shared instance (a logger, a connection pool) — the anti-pattern is using it as a smuggled **global variable**.

- Symptoms: hidden dependencies, hard-to-test code, shared mutable state causing order-dependent bugs.
- Fix: pass the dependency explicitly (constructor/parameter) instead of reaching for a static instance — see [dependency-injection](dependency-injection).

blocks.subTitle: Summary table
blocks.markdown:
Each smell has a well-known refactor.

| Smell | Typical fix |
|---|---|
| God Object | Extract Class |
| Long Method | Extract Method |
| Feature Envy | Move Method |
| Data Clumps | Introduce Parameter Object |
| Magic Numbers | Replace with named constant |

Memorize the *fix*, not just the *name* — interviews probe both.

blocks.subTitle: Feature Envy, refactored

blocks.markdown:
A smell is a **signal**, not a verdict. Context can make the "smelly" choice the right one.

- A short script's God Object may be fine; a shared library's is a liability.
- Chasing every smell wastes time — weigh churn, team size, and how long the code will live.
- Rule of thumb: refactor when the smell is actively slowing down a change you're already making.

Common mistakes when applying this:

- **Refactoring without tests.** A smell fix that breaks behavior is worse than the smell.
- **Treating every anti-pattern as intentional sabotage.** Most arrive from reasonable short-term choices under deadline pressure.
- **Over-engineering to avoid smells.** Adding layers to dodge a Long Method can create needless indirection — see [design-principles](design-principles).

blocks.subTitle: God Object
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a God Object and how do you fix it?**

A class that has absorbed too many responsibilities — it knows about and controls most of the system. Fix by identifying its distinct responsibilities and extracting each into its own class, then having the original delegate to them.

blocks.subTitle: Smell vs anti-pattern
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the difference between a code smell and an anti-pattern?**

A smell is a small, local hint inside a method or class that something could be cleaner. An anti-pattern is a bigger, named mistake in overall structure or process that looked like a good idea at the time. Smells often accumulate into anti-patterns if left unaddressed.

blocks.subTitle: Singleton as anti-pattern
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is Singleton sometimes called an anti-pattern?**

Not because the pattern itself is wrong, but because it's frequently misused as a global variable — hiding dependencies, making unit tests hard to isolate, and letting unrelated code mutate shared state. The fix is usually dependency injection instead of a static accessor.

blocks.subTitle: Naming smells
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Name a few common code smells you watch for.**

God Object, Long Method, Long Parameter List, Feature Envy, Duplicated Code, Shotgun Surgery, Primitive Obsession, Magic Numbers, and Data Clumps — each has a standard refactor, like Extract Method or Move Method.

blocks.subTitle: What is refactoring
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is refactoring, precisely?**

Changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behavior — same inputs, same outputs, cleaner implementation. It's the standard response to a code smell, and it only counts as refactoring if tests still pass before and after.
